name: Femoral neck stress fracture
aka: fatigue fracture of the femoral neck
populations: female athletes with low energy availability
summary: A fatigue fracture of the femoral neck from repetitive loading, usually in runners and recruits. Tension-side fractures can displace and cause avascular necrosis, so suspected cases need urgent MRI.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Compression-side, low grade: about 6–14 weeks; after fixation: 3–6+ months

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Graded return to running once walking and hopping are pain-free and imaging shows healing

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No accurate clinical test; groin pain on hopping or weight-bearing should prompt MRI

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs often normal early; MRI is the definitive investigation

keyFacts.label: Risk
keyFacts.value: High-risk site: delayed diagnosis increases displacement, AVN and career-ending outcomes

overview:
A femoral neck stress fracture (FNSF) is a bone stress injury caused by repetitive loading of a generally normal femoral neck. It accounts for about 3% of sport-related stress fractures and is seen mostly in long-distance runners, marathoners and military recruits [r1]. Bone stress injuries sit on a continuum from stress reaction to stress fracture and, if loading continues, complete fracture [r2]. The femoral neck is a high-risk site because the superolateral (tension) cortex heals poorly and a displaced fracture threatens the blood supply to the femoral head [r3,r4].

The typical presentation is exercise-related groin or anterior hip pain that is easily mistaken for a muscle strain or FAI. Diagnosis is often delayed, and delay increases the likelihood of displacement and poor sporting outcome [r1]. Management is guided by fracture location and extent: compression-side, incomplete fractures are usually managed with protected weight-bearing and graded loading, while tension-side, complete or extensive fractures are fixed surgically [r2,r4]. The physiotherapist's roles are early recognition and urgent referral, then a criteria-based return to loading that addresses the cause, including low energy availability [r5,r7].

epidemiology.text: FNSFs account for about 3% of sport-related stress fractures, most commonly from marathon and long-distance running [r1]. In a 4-year prospective military series, 54 femoral neck stress fractures occurred among 1,049 stress fractures of all types [r3]. Military recruits in basic training are a high-risk group, and a previous stress fracture increases the risk of another [r6]. Low energy availability (REDs) affects bone health in both female and male athletes [r7]. In collegiate track and field athletes, women with oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea had higher-grade bone stress injuries, and injuries at trabecular-rich sites such as the femoral neck took longer to return to sport [r8].

intrinsic: Low energy availability (REDs), menstrual dysfunction and low bone mineral density (modifiable) [r7,r8]
Female sex and lower aerobic fitness at the start of training [r6]
Low vitamin D and calcium intake (modifiable) [r5]
Coxa vara or other hip morphology that increases neck bending (proposed)
extrinsic: Rapid increase in running volume or intensity, or marching and load carriage in recruits [r5,r6]
Hard surfaces and high-impact running technique (low step rate, high impact loading) [r5]

mechanism.summary: With each foot strike, body weight and muscle forces bend the femoral neck in the frontal plane: the inferomedial cortex is compressed and the superolateral cortex is placed in tension. Thousands of submaximal loading cycles create microdamage faster than targeted remodelling can repair it, so bone resorption temporarily exceeds formation and the neck weakens [r2,r5]. Compression-side injuries begin at the inferomedial neck; tension-side injuries start superolaterally, where crack propagation and poor healing make displacement more likely [r4].
sequence: The athlete increases training load (more distance, speed or marching) without enough recovery or energy intake.
Each stance phase loads the hip with a multiple of body weight; the femoral neck bends like a cantilever.
The inferomedial cortex is compressed and the superolateral cortex is stretched with every stride.
Microcracks accumulate. Remodelling starts by resorbing damaged bone, which briefly makes the neck weaker [r2,r5].
A stress reaction (marrow oedema, periosteal response) develops and causes deep groin pain with running.
If loading continues, a fracture line forms: on the compression side it tends to stay stable; on the tension side it can propagate across the neck [r4].
Complete fracture and displacement can follow, disrupting the femoral head's blood supply [r12].

variants.name: Compression-side (inferomedial)
variants.description: The commonest type in young athletes. Starts as endosteal sclerosis or a small fracture line on the inferior neck. Lower risk, usually managed non-operatively if the line is limited.

variants.name: Tension-side (superolateral)
variants.description: Starts on the superior neck, where tensile stresses and poor healing favour progression. Usually managed with internal fixation [r4,r6].

variants.name: Displaced fracture
variants.description: A complete, displaced fracture is an orthopaedic emergency with high rates of avascular necrosis, nonunion and career-ending outcomes [r12].

variants.name: Insufficiency fracture
variants.description: In older or osteoporotic adults, normal loads cause a femoral neck fracture through weakened bone.

anatomy.text: The femoral neck joins the head to the shaft at a neck–shaft angle of about 125–135°. In the frontal plane it acts as a cantilever: weight-bearing loads compress its inferomedial cortex (calcar region) and tension its superolateral cortex. The neck is rich in trabecular bone arranged along compressive and tensile trabecular lines. The femoral head receives most of its blood supply from retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery that run along the superior and posterior neck within the capsule, so a displaced neck fracture can tear these vessels.

structures.name: Femoral neck (inferomedial cortex)
structures.role: Compression side; site of compression-type stress fractures

structures.name: Femoral neck (superolateral cortex)
structures.role: Tension side; site of high-risk tension-type stress fractures [r4]

structures.name: Trabecular bone of the neck
structures.role: Transmits load along trabecular lines; trabecular-rich sites recover more slowly [r8]

structures.name: Retinacular vessels (medial circumflex femoral artery)
structures.role: Main blood supply to the femoral head; at risk with displacement

structures.name: Hip abductors and gluteal muscles
structures.role: Generate compressive force across the neck and help dampen bending; fatigue may increase bone strain

structures.name: Hip capsule
structures.role: Encloses the neck; effusion can accompany more extensive stress injuries [r11]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
Bone adapts to load through targeted remodelling: osteoclasts remove microdamaged bone and osteoblasts replace it. A bone stress injury develops when microdamage accumulates faster than it can be removed and replaced [r2]. Because resorption precedes formation by weeks, a sudden increase in load can transiently weaken the bone just as loading rises [r5]. The result is a continuum from stress reaction (marrow oedema, periosteal reaction) to a stress fracture line and, eventually, complete fracture [r5].

At the femoral neck, tensile forces and relative avascularity at the superolateral cortex lead to poor healing, making tension-side fractures prone to progression [r4]. In military trainees who needed surgery, the fracture line progressed on repeat imaging in 39%, and the extent of oedema on initial T1-weighted MRI combined with a hip effusion correlated with the final fracture extent (r = 0.62) [r11]. Low energy availability suppresses bone formation and lowers bone mineral density, so the same training load causes more damage [r7,r8].

structures.name: Femoral neck cortex and trabeculae
structures.effect: Microdamage, marrow oedema, then a fracture line on the compression or tension side [r2]

structures.name: Periosteum and endosteum
structures.effect: Reactive new bone formation (endosteal sclerosis, periosteal callus) seen on later radiographs

structures.name: Hip joint
structures.effect: Reactive effusion with more extensive injury; associated with a larger final fracture extent [r11]

structures.name: Femoral head blood supply
structures.effect: Threatened if the fracture displaces, leading to avascular necrosis [r12]

muscles.name: Hip abductors (gluteus medius/minimus)
muscles.effect: Pain inhibition and disuse during protected weight-bearing cause rapid weakness and an antalgic or Trendelenburg gait

muscles.name: Hip flexors and adductors
muscles.effect: Guarding and pain on resisted testing can mimic a muscle strain, contributing to diagnostic delay [r1]

muscles.name: Calf and quadriceps
muscles.effect: Deconditioning during unloading; must be rebuilt before return to running [r5]

cellular.description: Linear microcracks form in cortical and trabecular bone, triggering osteocyte apoptosis around the cracks.
Osteocyte signalling recruits osteoclasts; resorption cavities transiently increase porosity and weaken the neck [r2,r5].
Marrow oedema and periosteal or endosteal reaction appear on MRI before any fracture line [r8].
A fracture line forms; on the tension side it can propagate across the neck [r4].
With load reduction, osteoblasts fill resorption spaces with woven bone that is remodelled to lamellar bone over months.

systems.effect: Low energy availability lowers oestrogen (or testosterone), IGF-1 and other bone-anabolic signals, reducing bone formation and density (REDs) [r7].
Periosteal and marrow nociceptors produce deep, poorly localised groin pain that is often misattributed to muscle [r1].
Retinacular vessels supplying the femoral head are vulnerable to displacement, leading to avascular necrosis [r12].
Enforced unloading, threat to selection or career, and possible disordered eating require sensitive screening and support [r7].
Weeks of protected weight-bearing cause widespread deconditioning that must be rebuilt before impact loading resumes [r5].

grades.description: Stress reaction or fracture line on the inferior neck not crossing the neck [r3]. Kaeding–Miller grade II (pain, no fracture line) or III (non-displaced fracture) [r9].
grades.prognosis: Usually heals with protected weight-bearing; extensive lines (>50% neck width) are often fixed [r11]

grades.description: Fracture line or cortical lucency on the superior neck [r3].
grades.prognosis: High risk of progression; internal fixation usually recommended [r4,r6]

grades.description: Complete fracture with displacement (Kaeding–Miller grade IV) [r3,r9].
grades.prognosis: Emergency fixation; high rates of AVN, nonunion and career loss [r12]

timeframes.summary: Healing follows bone biology: resorption and repair over 6–12 weeks, with remodelling for months. Time to return to sport is longer for higher MRI grades, lower bone density and trabecular-rich sites such as the femoral neck [r8].

healing.description: Protected weight-bearing; damaged bone is resorbed; pain settles
New bone fills resorption spaces and the fracture line; graded loading begins once walking is pain-free
Woven bone remodels to lamellar bone along load lines; impact tolerance returns progressively

milestones.label: Start walk–run program
milestones.note: Once hopping is pain-free and the treating doctor confirms healing

milestones.label: Return to running after fixation
milestones.note: Typical clinical range 3–6 months, per surgeon

timeframes.returnToSport: Compression-side, low-grade injuries: typically 6–14 weeks to graded running and 3–4 months to full training. Tension-side or fixed fractures: often 4–6+ months. Higher MRI grade, low bone density and trabecular sites prolong recovery [r8].

symptoms: Insidious, activity-related groin, anterior hip or anterior thigh pain, sometimes referred to the knee [r1]
Pain that starts during running and then occurs earlier, with walking, and eventually at rest or at night
Recent increase in training load, change of program or basic training [r5,r6]
Possible REDs features: menstrual disturbance, weight loss, restricted eating, fatigue, previous stress fractures [r7]
Sudden severe pain and inability to weight-bear suggest displacement
signs: Antalgic gait; pain on single-leg stance or hopping on the affected side
Pain at end-range hip flexion and internal rotation
Little or no local tenderness (the neck is deep)
Pain on log roll or with axial loading in more advanced injury
Normal or only mildly reduced strength with pain inhibition

subjective: Training history: recent changes in volume, intensity, surface, footwear, or start of basic training [r5,r6]
Pain behaviour: onset during activity, progression to walking or night pain, and any sudden worsening
REDs screen: energy intake, menstrual history, weight change, disordered eating, low bone density, previous bone stress injuries [r7]
Medical history: corticosteroids, endocrine disease, vitamin D status
Psychosocial context: selection pressure, career impact, mood
Goals and upcoming competition or training milestones
observation: Reluctance to weight-bear fully on the affected leg
General body composition and signs of low energy availability
palpation: Usually no focal tenderness because the neck is deep; absence of tenderness does not exclude FNSF
Palpate adductor, iliopsoas and pubic regions to identify alternative diagnoses
rangeOfMotion: Hip flexion and internal rotation: end-range pain is common
Log roll: pain suggests intra-articular or femoral neck pathology
Do not force painful end range if FNSF is suspected
strength: Gentle isometric testing only if FNSF is suspected; pain inhibition is common
Once healed, hand-held dynamometry of hip abduction, extension and flexion
functional: Single-leg stance and single-leg hop: pain in the groin is a strong reason to stop and image (do not repeat if painful)

specialTests.name: Single-leg hop test
specialTests.purpose: Provoke pain from a lower-limb bone stress injury
specialTests.procedure: Ask the patient to hop gently on the affected leg a few times. Stop at the first sign of pain.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of groin or hip pain. A positive test warrants imaging before any further loading.

specialTests.name: Log roll
specialTests.purpose: Low-load test for femoral neck or intra-articular pathology
specialTests.procedure: Patient supine with legs straight. Gently roll the thigh into internal and external rotation.

specialTests.name: Therapeutic ultrasound and tuning-fork tests
specialTests.purpose: Proposed bedside tests for lower-limb stress fractures
specialTests.procedure: Apply therapeutic ultrasound or a vibrating tuning fork over the suspected site.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of local pain. These tests are not accurate enough to rule a stress fracture in or out; use imaging.

outcomeMeasures.name: Pain-free walking and hopping (functional milestones)
outcomeMeasures.use: Gate progression through each loading stage [r5]

outcomeMeasures.name: REDs Clinical Assessment Tool – Version 2 (REDs CAT2)
outcomeMeasures.use: Assess severity and risk of low energy availability and guide training recommendations [r7]

outcomeMeasures.name: HAGOS (Copenhagen Hip and Groin Outcome Score)
outcomeMeasures.use: Hip and groin symptoms and function during return to sport

imaging.modality: Plain radiographs (AP pelvis and lateral hip)
imaging.indication: First-line investigation for exercise-related hip pain [r1]
imaging.findings: Often normal early. Later: endosteal sclerosis, callus or a fracture line on the inferior (compression) or superior (tension) neck; displacement

imaging.indication: Investigation of choice when FNSF is suspected and radiographs are normal; also grades severity [r1,r8]
imaging.findings: Marrow oedema (stress reaction), fracture line and its percentage of neck width, side (compression or tension), effusion [r11]

imaging.indication: Define the fracture line and healing when MRI is equivocal or before return to running
Recurrent bone stress injuries, trabecular-site injury or REDs risk factors [r7,r8]
imaging.findings: Low bone mineral density for age

differentials.name: FAI syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Groin pain with flexion–rotation and positive FADIR, but no pain with hopping or weight-bearing and no recent load spike. MRI distinguishes them.

differentials.name: Adductor-related groin pain
differentials.distinguishing: Tenderness at the adductor longus origin and pain on resisted adduction; hopping pain is less prominent.

differentials.name: Iliopsoas-related groin pain
differentials.distinguishing: Pain with resisted hip flexion and iliopsoas stretch, with tenderness below the inguinal ligament.

differentials.name: Pubic ramus stress fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Pain and tenderness at the inferior pubic ramus or buttock; also seen in female distance runners. MRI distinguishes.

differentials.name: Hip labral tear
differentials.distinguishing: Mechanical symptoms (clicking, catching); hopping is usually pain-free.

differentials.name: Bone stress injury and RED-S
differentials.distinguishing: Overarching condition: screen for other bone stress injuries and REDs in every athlete with an FNSF.

differentials.name: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
differentials.distinguishing: Steroid or alcohol use, sickle cell disease; MRI shows a subchondral necrotic segment rather than a neck fracture line.

redFlags: Groin pain on hopping, weight-bearing or at night in a runner or recruit: stop impact loading, start crutches and arrange urgent MRI the same week.
Sudden severe groin pain, inability to weight-bear or a shortened, externally rotated leg: suspect a displaced fracture. Keep non-weight-bearing and send to emergency immediately.
A tension-side fracture line, complete fracture or fracture line involving more than about half of the neck width: same-day orthopaedic referral for fixation [r4,r11].
Signs of REDs (amenorrhoea, weight loss, disordered eating, recurrent bone stress injuries): refer to a sports physician and dietitian; consider bone density assessment [r7].
Bilateral or multiple bone stress injuries, or fracture with minimal loading: investigate for metabolic bone disease.

management.principles:
Suspect FNSF early in any runner or recruit with exercise-related groin pain, stop impact loading and obtain MRI if radiographs are normal [r1]. Management is set by the doctor or surgeon according to the side and extent of the fracture [r2]. Compression-side injuries without an extensive fracture line are treated with protected weight-bearing on crutches until walking is pain-free, followed by a slow, criteria-based return to loading. Tension-side, complete or extensive compression-side fractures, and any progression on repeat imaging, are treated with internal fixation; displaced fractures are emergencies [r4,r6,r11].

The physiotherapist coordinates the return to loading and addresses the cause: training-load errors, running technique, muscle capacity and, critically, low energy availability, which needs a multidisciplinary approach with a sports physician and dietitian [r5,r7]. Recovery is slower at the femoral neck and with lower bone density, so expectations should be set early [r8].

medical.name: Protected weight-bearing and activity restriction (compression-side, incomplete)
medical.description: Crutches with toe-touch or partial weight-bearing until pain-free walking (typically 3–6 weeks), then progressive loading; repeat imaging if pain persists or worsens [r2,r6].

medical.name: Internal fixation (cannulated screws or sliding hip screw)
medical.description: Indicated for tension-side, complete or displaced fractures and high-risk compression-side fractures (generally >50% of neck width) or fracture-line progression [r4,r11].

medical.name: Emergency reduction and fixation of a displaced fracture
medical.description: Urgent surgery to reduce and stabilise the fracture and protect the femoral head blood supply. Complications (AVN, nonunion, refracture) are common [r12].

medical.name: Treatment of REDs and bone health
medical.description: Restore energy availability, address menstrual dysfunction, ensure adequate calcium and vitamin D, and assess bone density where indicated [r7].

medical.name: NSAIDs for bone pain
medical.description: May impair bone healing; simple analgesia (paracetamol) is preferred during the healing phase.

physio.name: Early recognition, load cessation and referral
physio.description: Stop running and impact loading, issue crutches and refer for imaging and medical management when FNSF is suspected. Delay increases displacement and worsens outcomes [r1,r12].

physio.name: Graded, criteria-based return to loading
physio.description: Progress from protected walking to full walking, then hopping, a walk–run program and finally speed and volume, each stage gated by pain-free function [r5].

physio.name: Non-impact cross-training
physio.description: Upper-body work, swimming (pull buoy) and, once walking is pain-free, cycling or deep-water running to maintain fitness without loading the neck, as cleared by the doctor.

physio.name: Hip and lower-limb strengthening
physio.description: Progressive hip abductor, extensor and calf strengthening to restore capacity lost during unloading [r5].

physio.name: Running retraining and training-load planning
physio.description: Increase step rate, run 'softer' and plan gradual load progressions to reduce bone loading [r5].

physio.name: Clinical bedside tests to confirm or exclude fracture
physio.description: Therapeutic ultrasound and tuning-fork tests are not accurate enough to diagnose a stress fracture; imaging is required [r10].

physio.name: Running through pain
physio.description: Continuing to load a painful femoral neck risks progression to complete or displaced fracture [r1,r12].

education: This is a crack in the neck of the thigh bone from repeated loading. Most heal well if found early, but continuing to run on it can cause a complete fracture.
Use crutches exactly as advised. Pain-free walking is the first goal; running comes later and step by step.
Energy intake matters. Bone needs enough fuel to heal and stay strong, so we will look at nutrition and, for women, menstrual health.
Report sudden severe pain or inability to put weight through the leg immediately; this is an emergency.
A planned, gradual return to running and smarter training load reduce the chance of it happening again.

rehab.overview: Rehabilitation is criteria-based and led by pain-free function, imaging and the medical team's decisions [r5]. Stages below describe a compression-side, non-operative pathway; after fixation follow the surgeon's weight-bearing protocol and progress more slowly. Pain must be 0/10 during and after each loading step before progressing; any return of groin pain means stepping back and seeking review. Address the cause in parallel: training-load plan, running technique and REDs [r5,r7].

stages.name: Protect & unload
goals: Maintain cardiovascular fitness without hip impact
Start REDs assessment and nutritional support
precautions: No running, jumping or single-leg hopping
Weight-bearing as prescribed (often toe-touch to partial)
No forced end-range hip flexion and internal rotation
Stop any exercise that causes groin pain

exercises.name: Upper-body and core conditioning (e.g. dead bug)
Swimming with pull buoy or upper-body ergometer

progressionCriteria: Pain-free walking without crutches for 30 min
Medical clearance based on clinical progress ± imaging

stages.name: Restore walking & strength
goals: Full pain-free walking and daily activity
Rebuild hip, thigh and calf strength
precautions: Increase walking volume gradually (e.g. 10–20% per week)

exercises.name: Side-lying clamshell progressing to side plank

progressionCriteria: Hip strength ≥80% of the other side
Pain-free single-leg hopping 10–20 times (test only when cleared)

stages.name: Impact & return to running
goals: Address running technique and training plan
precautions: Any groin pain during or after running: stop and step back one level
Increase only one variable (time, then speed) at a time

exercises.name: Walk–run intervals (e.g. 1 min run / 1 min walk × 10)
exercises.dosage: Alternate days, progressing to 30 min continuous

progressionCriteria: 30 min continuous easy running pain-free on alternate days
Hip strength ≥90% of the other side
Healing confirmed by the medical team where required

stages.name: Return to performance
goals: Rebuild weekly volume and introduce speed work
Return to racing or full military training
precautions: Increase weekly volume gradually, avoiding spikes
Monitor energy availability and menstrual function throughout

exercises.name: Progressive run program (volume, then intensity)
exercises.dosage: Per plan, with easy weeks every 3–4 weeks

exercises.name: Heavy strength maintenance (squat, split squat, RDL, calf raise)

progressionCriteria: Pre-injury training volume tolerated without pain
Shared decision with athlete, coach and medical team

criteria: Pain-free walking, hopping and daily activities
Healing confirmed by the treating doctor or surgeon (clinical ± imaging)
Completion of a graded walk–run program to 30+ min continuous running without pain
Hip and lower-limb strength ≥90% of the other side
REDs risk addressed, with adequate energy availability [r7]
Training plan with gradual progression agreed with athlete and coach [r5]

prognosis: Early-diagnosed compression-side fractures generally heal with non-operative care and have good return-to-sport rates [r1]. Outcomes are much worse after displacement: in one series of 23 athletes with a mean diagnostic delay of 14 weeks, 30% developed complications needing major surgery, three developed avascular necrosis and every elite athlete ended their career [r12]. In military trainees who required surgery, 58% were medically separated from service [r11]. Higher MRI grade, lower bone density and trabecular-rich sites such as the femoral neck predict longer recovery [r8]. Recurrence is common unless underlying causes such as training errors and low energy availability are corrected [r5,r7].
prevention: Plan gradual increases in training volume and intensity, with recovery weeks, and avoid sudden load spikes [r5].
Ensure adequate energy availability, calcium and vitamin D; screen at-risk athletes for REDs [r7].
Educate runners, coaches and recruits that groin pain on running or hopping needs early assessment [r1].
Improve pre-training fitness in recruits and progress marching and load-carriage gradually [r6].
Running technique changes that reduce impact (higher step rate, 'softer' running) may lower bone loading [r5].
clinicalPearls: Groin pain on hopping in a runner is a femoral neck stress fracture until MRI proves otherwise. Do not let them run while waiting.
Plain X-rays are often normal early. Order or request MRI rather than relying on radiographs [r1].
Tension-side (superolateral) fractures are surgical. Know which side the fracture is on before planning rehab [r4].
Every FNSF should trigger a REDs screen, in men as well as women [r7].
The neck is deep, so there is usually no point tenderness. Lack of tenderness is not reassurance.
Expect slower recovery than for tibial or metatarsal stress fractures; trabecular sites take longer [r8].

animation.title: How a femoral neck stress fracture develops

captions.text: A distance runner has increased weekly mileage quickly while not eating enough to match training.
Each foot strike loads the hip; the femoral neck bends like a cantilever thousands of times per run.
Microcracks form faster than remodelling can repair them: load now exceeds bone capacity.
Deep groin pain starts with running, then with walking. The runner slows to a limp.
Zooming into the right femoral neck from the front.
In stance, the femoral neck bends: its lower border is compressed and its upper border stretched.
Compression-side stress reaction: marrow oedema at the inferior neck. Usually stable if caught early.
On the tension side, the superior cortex is pulled apart and heals poorly.
A fracture line forms superiorly. It can propagate across the neck and displace.
A hip effusion may accompany more extensive injury.
Displacement can tear the vessels to the femoral head, so this injury needs urgent MRI and protection.
Healthy bone: osteocytes sense strain and direct remodelling.
Repetitive running loads bend the bone thousands of times.
Linear microcracks accumulate in the cortex and trabeculae.
Osteoclasts remove damaged bone first, so the neck is briefly weaker.
Stress reaction: marrow oedema and periosteal response cause pain.
With continued loading, cracks join into a fracture line.
With unloading and enough energy intake, osteoblasts fill the gaps and the bone remodels.
